title: Where Did American Savings Go? The $1.1 Trillion Credit Surge

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: In early 2020, lockdown life sparked an unprecedented surge in household thrift across the country. In April 2020, the personal saving rate hit a staggering record of 31.8%.

segments.label: scene 2 (statement)
segments.text: For a brief moment, American households sat on a massive financial shield of unspent cash.

segments.label: scene 3 (waffle)
segments.text: But as life reopened and inflation took hold, those built-up reserves quickly melted away.

segments.label: scene 4 (counter)
segments.text: Today, the economic script has flipped entirely. By October 2026, credit card balances at U.S. banks hit a record $1.1 trillion.

segments.label: scene 5 (compare)
segments.text: Rather than stashing money into bank accounts, consumers are increasingly relying on high-interest credit cards to make ends meet.

segments.label: scene 6 (multiline)
segments.text: While average pay has steadily climbed, borrowing balances expanded even faster over the exact same period.

segments.label: scene 7 (gauge)
segments.text: How did America swing from the greatest saving frenzy in modern history to an unprecedented pile of debt? Let's unpack where the money actually went.

segments.label: scene 8 (statement)
segments.text: To fully understand why savings dissolved, we need to trace where the pre-pandemic baseline originally started back in 2015.

segments.label: scene 9 (counter)
segments.text: In January 2015, the personal saving rate sat at 6.3% of disposable income, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

segments.label: scene 10 (line)
segments.text: Household saving was resilient. By September 2018, the saving rate climbed to 6.8%, marking a 15% increase over the preceding year.

segments.label: scene 11 (compare)
segments.text: Wages laid a foundation for that growth. Non-managerial workers earned an average hourly pay of $20.80 in January 2015.

segments.label: scene 12 (gauge)
segments.text: Borrowing was also far lower than modern levels. U.S. banks held $625.5 billion in credit card balances in January 2015.

segments.label: scene 13 (multiline)
segments.text: Across this pre-2020 period, rising pay supported manageable debt levels without eroding everyday bank accounts.

segments.label: scene 14 (statement)
segments.text: This balanced dynamic established a stable financial environment for American households right before the shocks of 2020 arrived.

segments.label: scene 15 (statement)
segments.text: As stimulus checks faded and post-pandemic inflation took hold, America's newfound financial safety net vanished rapidly.

segments.label: scene 16 (counter)
segments.text: By June 2022, the personal saving rate crashed to an historic low of just 2.4%.

segments.label: scene 17 (compare)
segments.text: That marked a devastating slide. From its record peak in April 2020 down to September 2026, the saving rate plunged 88%.

segments.label: scene 18 (heatmap)
segments.text: The momentum downwards has not stopped. Between September 2025 and September 2026, saving rates fell another 25.5% over that single year.

segments.label: scene 19 (line)
segments.text: To fill the expanding gap, households turned heavily to plastic. Credit card balances at U.S. banks climbed 76% from January 2015 to October 2026.

segments.label: scene 20 (compare)
segments.text: Borrowing kept accelerating up to the present day. Credit balances grew another 4.2% over the last year, between October 2025 and October 2026.

segments.label: scene 21 (multiline)
segments.text: Even as average hourly pay reached $32.75 in October 2026, high debt balances eroded the remaining buffer for everyday consumers.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Government stimulus disbursements initially flooded household bank accounts with direct relief, creating an artificial surge in liquid cash.

segments.label: scene 23 (bars)
segments.text: Yet when economy-wide reopenings began, severe supply chain bottlenecks met intense consumer demand, unleashing widespread cost inflation.

segments.label: scene 24 (line)
segments.text: As everyday expenses climbed, liquid cushions evaporated. From January 2020 to September 2026, the personal saving rate plunged 44%.

segments.label: scene 25 (counter)
segments.text: To sustain spending, consumers turned back to debt. In January 2020, before the crisis unfolded, credit card balances at U.S. banks stood at $848.5 billion.

segments.label: scene 26 (line)
segments.text: As price tags expanded across retail sectors, those total credit card balances surged 29% from January 2020 to October 2026.

segments.label: scene 27 (line)
segments.text: On the earnings side, labor tightness pushed nominal pay upward. Non-managerial workers earned an average hourly pay of $23.91 back in January 2020.

segments.label: scene 28 (bars)
segments.text: Average pay climbed 37% by October 2026. However, because structural inflation eroded purchasing power, higher wages couldn't prevent savings from drying up.

segments.label: scene 29 (statement)
segments.text: Higher hourly wages provided essential relief to working families across America, yet mounting monthly obligations continuously squeezed household budgets.

segments.label: scene 30 (line)
segments.text: Non-managerial hourly pay expanded by 57% between January 2015 and October 2026, pushing nominal paychecks significantly higher over the decade.

segments.label: scene 31 (waffle)
segments.text: Despite those earnings gains, total household debt service payments still consumed 11.1% of disposable income in April 2026.

segments.label: scene 32 (line)
segments.text: Emergency stimulus measures and reduced spending temporarily drove that debt payment burden down to an historic low of 9.1% in January 2021.

segments.label: scene 33 (counter)
segments.text: As post-pandemic financial conditions stabilized, total debt burdens plateaued, dropping just 0.1% over the year to 11.1% in April 2026.

segments.label: scene 34 (statement)
segments.text: Because fixed interest payments continuously claim a major slice of earnings, hourly pay raises get absorbed before building long-term cash reserves.

segments.label: scene 35 (kpi)
segments.text: This delicate tension between rising hourly pay and persistent debt service obligations explains why everyday family finances remain under constant pressure.

segments.label: scene 36 (line)
segments.text: Over the last decade, the safety cushion for American households steadily shrank. From January 2015 to September 2026, the personal saving rate dropped by 40%.

segments.label: scene 37 (counter)
segments.text: Today, families hold onto far less of their income each month. By September 2026, the saving rate stood at just 3.8%.

segments.label: scene 38 (compare)
segments.text: That decline accelerated again recently. Between January 2025 and September 2026, the saving rate fell by 33%.

segments.label: scene 39 (statement)
segments.text: High prices continuously drain cash, forcing households to rely on credit cards rather than true liquid reserves.

segments.label: scene 40 (bars)
segments.text: Credit card balances grew another 5% from January 2025 to October 2026, locking in high fixed expenses.

segments.label: scene 41 (kpi)
segments.text: The key takeaway is clear: higher wages have not restored long-term financial security. Has your household buffer changed over recent years? Tell us in the comments.

segments.label: scene 42 (statement)
segments.text: Subscribe to Plotline Data for more data-driven stories on the economy.
